question.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})j \\  & =(2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2x)i+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)+2y)j \\ ∇f(1,0) & =(2(1)(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))-2(1))i+((1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))+2(0))j \\  & =-2\,i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,0)=⟨-2,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{-2} & =\frac{y-0}{1} \\ x-1 & =-2y \\ x+2y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$
